An Asscher cut diamond is `a square, step-cut stone with clipped corners that create a signature "hall of mirrors" geometric effect`.[[1]](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/)[[2]](https://filigreejewelers.com/blogs/articles/asscher-cut-engagement-rings)

### Key Characteristics

- **Facets:** Traditional Asscher cuts have 58 step-cut facets, while the patented [Royal Asscher](https://royalasscher.com/) features 74 facets for extra brilliance.[[1]](https://filigreejewelers.com/blogs/articles/asscher-cut-engagement-rings)[[2]](https://www.tiktok.com/@thejewelstandard/video/7616131922963582238)
- **Shape:** It is nearly square with deeply cropped, octagonal corners. Look for a length-to-width ratio close to 1.00 for a true square.[[1]](https://www.rarecarat.com/education/shape/the-asscher-cut)[[2]](https://www.whiteflash.com/diamond-education/diamond-shapes/asscher-cut/)[[3]](https://filigreejewelers.com/blogs/articles/asscher-cut-engagement-rings)
- **Clarity Focus:** Because step cuts have open, transparent tables, inclusions are easier to see. A VS2 or higher clarity grade is typically recommended.[[1]](https://www.laurenbjewelry.com/asscher-cut-diamond-engagement-rings)[[2]](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYbis-iJwlf/?hl=en)
- **Size Appearance:** They are cut deep to maximize light depth, meaning they often face up slightly smaller than other diamond shapes of the same carat weight.[[1]](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYbis-iJwlf/?hl=en)

### Shopping and Pricing
Prices for Asscher cut diamonds vary based on whether they are natural or lab-grown, as well as their 4 Cs (cut, color, clarity, carat).[[1]](https://www.bluenile.com/diamonds/asscher-cut)

- **Lab-grown and smaller stones** can start around $250.
- **Natural mid-range stones** (such as 0.70 to 1.20 carats) generally range from $1,300 to $4,000+ depending on certification and quality.
- You can explore loose options or custom settings through retailers like [Blue Nile](https://www.bluenile.com/diamonds/asscher-cut) or [Brilliant Earth](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/).[[1]](https://www.google.com/search?q=product&prds=pvt:hg,productid:52662542212579935,catalogid:8141850162837992744,gpcid:7355059317661634280,mid:576462815832301427&ibp=oshop)[[2]](https://www.google.com/search?q=product&prds=pvt:hg,productid:16066868529979882588,catalogid:11631119645592145289&ibp=oshop)[[3]](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/)[[4]](https://www.bluenile.com/diamonds/asscher-cut)

If you are looking to shop or design a ring, let me know:

- Are you looking for a **natural or lab-grown** diamond?
- What is your target **carat size** and **budget**?
- Do you have a preferred **setting style** (solitaire, halo, three-stone)?

Fiancé’s Asscher!!!

An 8ct Early Asscher Cut

This is not how most Asscher Cuts look today.
This original early 20th-century example comes from a Boucheron ballerina ring and reflects a very different approach to the shape.

Instead of the flatter profile and larger table seen in many modern Asscher Cuts, this diamond is chunkier, with broader corners, a smaller table and more substantial proportions.

That early construction changes the way the stone handles light. The reflections feel broader, deeper and less graphic than those of a modern version, giving the diamond a heavier, more architectural presence.

The Boucheron setting is impressive, but for me, it almost competes with the stone.

I would rather see this diamond in something simpler—quiet enough to let the proportions, the geometry and the age of the cut do the work.

Sometimes an important diamond needs less around it, not more.

What would you do with it?

Joseph Asscher spent weeks mapping the Cullinan diamond before successfully splitting it on his second try. But the lore surrounding that moment is legendary in the jewellery trade.

For ages, the famous story was that the crushing psychological pressure was so overwhelming that the second the diamond sheared in two, Asscher lost consciousness and fainted on the floor of his workshop. 

In reality, his family later admitted the fainting story was a myth. He didn’t pass out. After successfully splitting the most valuable piece of rough diamond in human history, he calmly put down his tools, walked into the next room, and opened a bottle of champagne. What a baller.

But what actually happened to the yield of that historic hammer strike?
